extracted.intended_audience: printers, copyeditors, typesetters, proofreaders, and authors preparing manuscripts for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for hyphenation, word division, footnotes, indexing, tabular work, spacing, indentation, and other typographic/style practices for book and journal composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of adjectives formed with -like
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by the suffixation of "like" to a noun are usually printed as one word if the noun contains only one syllable; if it contains more (or is a proper noun), they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, warlike, godlike; eel-like, bell-like; woman-like, business-like; American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate certain title elements
rubrics_metrics.description: "Vice," "ex-," "elect," "general," and "lieutenant," constituting parts of titles, should be connected with the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of by- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds beginning with "by-" should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation with co-, pre-, re- when same vowel repeats
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes "co-," "pre-," and "re-" when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, take a hyphen; but as a rule they do not when followed by a different vowel or by a consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter; but: coequal, coeducation, prearranged, reinstall; cohabitation, prehistoric, recast (re-read). Note exceptions for proper names, long/unusual formations, and when omission would change meaning (pre-Raphaelite, re-cover (= cover again)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit hyphen in certain adverbial/time compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific commonly used temporal/compound adverbs are printed without a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: today, tomorrow, tonight, viewpoint, standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particle hyphenation rules (un-, in-, a-, non-)
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles "un-," "in-," and "a-" do not usually require a hyphen. The particle "non-" ordinarily calls for a hyphen, except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples without hyphen: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate, asyntmetrical. Examples with non-: non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-contagious; but common forms: nonage, nondescript, nonessential, nonsense, noncombatant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate quasi- prefixed words
rubrics_metrics.description: "Quasi" prefixed to a noun or an adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over- and under- prefix hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Over" and "under" prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in rare cases (e.g., lengthy words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, overweight, underfed, undersecretary; but exceptions include: over-soul, under-man, over-spiritualistic, over-search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin prepositional prefixes (ante-, anti-, inter-, intra-, post-, sub-, super-)
rubrics_metrics.description: These prefixes do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, antidote, antiseptic, international, interstate, intramural, postscript, postgraduate, subconscious, submarine, subtitle, subway, superfine. Exceptions: ante-bellum, ante-Nicene, anti-Semitic, inter-university, post-revolutionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation with extra-, infra-, supra-, ultra-
rubrics_metrics.description: "Extra," "infra," "supra," and "ultra" as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, supra-temporal, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation in spelled-out fractional numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect by a hyphen the numerator and the denominator, unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "two-thirds", four and five-sevenths, thirty-hundredths; exception: "one half" in constructions like "One half of his fortune..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of repeated element in adjacent compounds indicated by hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together have one component in common, the repeated element may be omitted from all but the last word and indicated by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces; note that some regard this hyphen as objectionable Teutonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate an incomplete prefix or suffix
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or a suffix, as a particle or syllable, not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "The prefix a-"; "The German diminutive suffixes -chen and -lein."

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen used to indicate syllable breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is employed to indicate the syllables of a word when showing pronunciation or division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of everyday words that should be hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific common words that do not fall under previous classifications are listed as hyphenated and should be printed with hyphens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (partial list): after-years, cross-section, man-of-war, son-in-law, bas-relief, death-rate, object-lesson, subject-matter, birth-rate, feast-day, page-proof, thought-process, blood-feud, folk-song, pay-roll, title-page, well-being, cross-reference, guinea-pig, sea-level, well-nigh, common-sense, fountain-head, post-office, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary word divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words; wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General admonition: prefer whole words to hyphenated divisions when spacing allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dividing very short syllables in wide measures
rubrics_metrics.description: In wide measures (20 ems or more) do not divide on a syllable of two letters if possible; words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six letters rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good spacing is paramount; avoid dividing minimal syllables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consecutive lines ending in hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen, if at all avoidable; avoid a divided word in the next-to-last line and ensure the last line (breakline) contains at least four letters in measures of 15 ems and up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also try to avoid a divided word at the bottom of a right-hand (recto) page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially names of persons, unless absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid splitting names across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not separate initials or common abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not separate (place in different lines) the initials of a name, or combinations like A.D., P.M., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep such units intact on one line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep divisional marks with the matter they precede
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the separation of a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (i)) from the section which it precedes; do not allow such mark to fall at the end of a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry the mark over with the matter to which it pertains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide words according to pronunciation (American system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide according to pronunciation, not according to derivation; as far as compatible with pronunciation and spacing, divide compounds on etymological lines or according to derivation and meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy not demo-cracy; knowledge not knowl-edge; dis-pleasure preferred to displeas-ure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division when two consonants meet between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels and the syllable ends on one consonant, the division may properly be made between the consonants; pronunciation determines the place of division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, finan-cier, moun-tain, profes-sor, struc-ture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid certain terminal consonant divisions (soft c, g, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c or similar awkward splits; escape the division entirely if possible; if impossible, divide as shown in examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred divisions: pro-cess (not proc-ess); ne-cessary (not nec-essary); spacing not spac-ing; pro-geny not prog-eny; pre-judice not prej-udice. (Rule differs from some dictionaries.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel where practicable; exceptions for -able/-dble
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel wherever practicable. Exceptions: words in -able and -dble should carry the vowel over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: separate (sepa-rate, not sep-arate); readable (read-able, not readarble); convertible (convert-ible, not converti-ble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens within already hyphenated words
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives avoid adding further hyphens across divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson not object-les-son; fellow-being not fel-low-being; poverty-stricken not pover-ty-stricken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat diphthongs as single letters in division
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel-sounds into one (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; therefore do not divide if there is any escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people (avoid peo-ple), Caesar (Cae-sar), ailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division in derivatives from words ending in -t depending on accent shift
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in t, the t in divisions should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has been shifted; if the derivative has retained the accent of the parent-word, leave the t in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); defect-ive (from defect').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural -s additions do not create new division opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a plural s, adding a new syllable to words ending in an 'e' sound, does not create a new excuse for dividing such words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of impossible divisions: hor-ses and drcumstan-ces (i.e., do not divide as 'drum-stan-ces' split oddly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of adjectives in -ical
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives in -ical should be divided on the i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: physi-cal, not phys-ical or physic-al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide the word 'nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide 'nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise rule: 'Do not divide nothing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: French syllabification/division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible, avoiding consonantal ending of syllables; two consonants of which the second is l or r (but not rl/ lr) are both carried over to the following syllable; there are as many syllables as vowels even if soundless, though a mute e following a vowel does not form a syllable; certain letters (f, y, o, u when preceding vowels) often act as consonants and do not form syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-té, a-che-ter; tableau (not tab-leau); bien, tions, yeux, fouetter, écuel-le.

rubrics_metrics.name: German syllabification/division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible; if several consonants stand between vowels, usually only the last is carried over; certain clusters (sch, ch, etc.) are generally separated except noted exceptions; if ck must be divided it is separated into k-k; compound words are separated into components first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hü-ten, Le-ben, Rit-ter, Klir-ren, Busche, Be-cher; Deckel — Dek-kel; Fürsten-schloss, Tür-an-gel, Inter-esse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian syllabification/division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; s before a consonant, r following a consonant, ch, ghi, gli, gn, sc, etc., are never separated; certain vowel groups are not separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-vo-li-no, mi-gliore, bi-sogno, in-chiostro, uscire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish syllabification/division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; ch, ll, rr, ñ are regarded as simple consonants and follow the rule; cc and nn are divided as in English; liquid consonants l and r, when preceded by a consonant other than s, must not be separated from that consonant except in compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les, ba-ta-lla, bu-llo, ac-ce-so, en-no-ble-cer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek syllabification/division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Single consonants, combinations that can begin a word, and mutes followed by liquids are placed at the beginning of a syllable; other consonant combinations are divided; compound words are divided into original parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (Greek examples shown in original orthography); compound division follows component parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin syllabification/division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as vowels or diphthongs; when a single consonant occurs between two vowels, divide before the consonant; when two or more consonants, divide before the last consonant except in mute+liquid combinations and qu/gu; compound words separated into elements first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es; om-nis, scrip-tus; ad-est, ab-rum-po, trans-i-go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of superior figures and symbols for footnote indices
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indices, as a rule, use superior figures. Only in special cases should asterisks, daggers, etc., be employed (for instance, in tabular or algebraic matter where figures might cause confusion). Index figures in text should be placed after punctuation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When figures are not used, sequence: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ibid. and other short citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use ibid. instead of repeating the title; ibid. takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ordinarily use ibid. for the first footnote on a verso page; better to repeat the title if short or use loc. cit. or op. cit.; examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes in tables formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables (ruled or open) should be in 6-pt and should be placed at the foot of the table and not at the foot of the page. For reference indices in tables use asterisks, etc., not superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules for use of symbols vs figures (232).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not repeat author's name in footnote if given in text
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference or quotation, it should not be repeated in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: This theory is questioned by Herbert, as follows: "..." (then footnote: Laws of the Ancients I, 153).

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of index figure relative to quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to place the index figure in the text after the quotation than before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in the manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and numeral styles in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit "Vol.", "chap.", and "p." in references to particular passages. Use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, and Division, except for ancient/classical works (use lower-case Roman numerals for chapters of classical works); Arabic numerals for number and text pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use abbreviations when confusion might arise; classical references use periods instead of commas to indicate divisions; examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date placement in periodical references
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of publication in a reference to a periodical should immediately follow the volume number and should be put in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example format shown in illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecutive footnote numbering in machine-set work
rubrics_metrics.description: In work set on the linotype machine, footnotes should be numbered consecutively through an article (or through a chapter in a book) to save resetting in case of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note exceptions for journals adopting different styles; examples of journals and their practices are listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: handling French/Belgian/Spanish name particles (le, la, du, des)
rubrics_metrics.description: A French, Belgian, or Spanish name preceded by "le," "la," "du," or "des" should be listed under the letters of the prefix in advance of the ordinary "L" or "D" list; if preceded by "de" or "d'" list under the first letter of the word following the prefix, placing the particle after the initials or Christian name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Conte, John; La Noue, Francois de; L'Estrange, Sir Roger; Du Maurier, George; Des Essarts, Jean; La Mancha, Don Quixote de. Note: if the particle is actually part of the surname, index by the particle (De Bey, De Quincey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: German 'von' names
rubrics_metrics.description: German names preceded by 'von' should be indexed according to the initials of the name following the prefix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sternthal, Max von; Goethe, J. W. von.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: M', Mac, Mc capitalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Names beginning with "M'", "Mac", or "Mc" with the following letter capitalized should be indexed in advance of the ordinary "M" list, each section arranged alphabetically according to the letters following the prefix. Names beginning with "Mac" without the following letter capitalized take their natural place in the M list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish capitalization after Mac/Mc when indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: O', St., Van capitalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Names preceded by "O'", "St.", or "Van" with the following letter capitalized should be placed in advance of the "O", "S" or "V" list and arranged alphabetically according to the letter following the prefix; those without capitalization take ordinary places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: O'Neil before O-..., Saint- Saens handled per French rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names joined by connectives (and, &, y, et, und, e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names or firms connected by "and", "&", "y" (Spanish), "et" (French), "und" (German), "e" (Italian) should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smith and Evans (under 'S'); Gomez y Pineda (under 'G'); Loubet et Meunier (under 'L').

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: hyphenated names
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated names should be listed according to the name following the hyphen if English; according to the name preceding the hyphen if French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Taylor, Henry Chandler- (for Henry Chandler-Taylor); Saint-Saens, Charles Camille (for Charles Camille Saint-Saens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: German umlauts treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: German names spelled with an Umlaut (Ä, Ö, Ü) should be indexed as if spelled with A, O, or U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index as if diacritic were absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: type sizes and leading conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In 11-pt. and 10-pt. matter open (unruled) tables should ordinarily be set in 9-pt. leaded; ruled, in 8-pt. solid. In 9-pt. matter both open and ruled tables should be set in 8-pt. solid. In 8-pt. matter open tables in 6-pt. leaded; ruled, in 6-pt. solid. In 6-pt. matter both open and ruled in 6-pt. solid. There is a practice of using different type in tables for totals, averages, percentages, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For differentiation use italic or black-face figures to set off classes of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular captions and box-heads sizing and styling
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. In ruled tables with box-heads of several stories, the upper (primary) heads should be set in caps and small caps (except where the second story consists of figures only); the lower (secondary) in caps and lower-case. Where small caps are used in box-heads, the stub head should also be set in caps and small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Styling guidance for multi-story box-heads and stub heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular spacing between rules and matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and if practicable at least the equivalent of an em-quad of the type in which the body of the table is set between vertical rules and the matter inclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear breathing space between rules and table content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-table column separators (periods or leaders)
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods, one em apart and aligned, or leaders may be used between the columns. In ruled tables, in the stub, leaders should usually be employed if there is room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'leader' (period or hyphen leader) and use appropriately in indexes and tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leaders to indicate blanks in numeric columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In columns of figures, to express a blank use leaders the width of the largest number in the column; center the figures in the column; if digits vary, leave more space on the left than on the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For four digits use a 2-em leader, etc.; always at least two dots in leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment and wrapping of reading-matter in table columns
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading-matter in the columns of a ruled table, it should be centered if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indention and align all on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer centered single-line items; use hanging indent for wrapped cells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double rules usage in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables, but vertical (perpendicular) double rules only when a table is doubled up on itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top-of-table emphasis via double rules; avoid vertical double rules unless table is doubled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vs ruled table decision by column count
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables of two columns only should be set as open; tables of three or more columns should be set as ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple two-column lists are open; more complex multi-column tables use rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table numbering and headline typography
rubrics_metrics.description: "Table I," etc., in headlines of tables should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set; the following descriptive line, if any, in caps and small caps of the same type. A single descriptive headline not preceded by the number should be set in caps of the type in which the table is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Styling conventions for numbered and unnumbered table headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point system and pica as unit of measure
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of typographical measures. The standard of measurement is the pica (12 points = one pica; one-sixth of an inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of common sizes: 12-pt (pica), 11-pt (small pica), 10-pt (long primer), 9-pt (bourgeois), 8-pt (brevier), 7-pt (minion), 6-pt (nonpareil), 5-pt (pearl). Sizes larger or smaller seldom used in book composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type styles: roman, italic, bold-face
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type is called roman. Type with a sloping face is italic. Type with a heavy black face is called bold-face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscript indications: straight line under words for italic; wavy line for bold-face; examples shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type anatomy and font components
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: the body of a type is called the shank; the upper surface bearing the character is the face; projecting parts are kern and shoulder. A font includes caps, small caps, and lower-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caps and small caps are indicated by manuscript marks; examples of caps, small caps, lower-case displayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype spacing system
rubrics_metrics.description: In monotype composition the 'unit' system (imits) instead of the pica system is used. There are fixed unit spaces (6-unit = 3-em space; 5-unit = 4-em space; 4-unit = little less than 5-em) cast from matrices; justification spreads spaces equitably when composing on keyboard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between fixed cast spaces and swelling/justifying spaces used during line composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linotype spacing system
rubrics_metrics.description: On the linotype machine the pica system of measurement is used. There are three fixed spaces: em-quad, en-quad, and thin space (equal to a 4-em space). To spread spaces a space band is used which can spread a space between specified sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a space smaller than a thin space is required it must be put in by hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of em, en, and other spaces/dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: An em (em-quad) is a square block equal to the type size; an en-quad is half an em; three-em, four-em, five-em spaces and hair-spaces are defined relative to the em; corresponding dashes (em-dash, en-dash, 2-em, 3-em) are defined by em multiples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative lines set with various quads and dashes shown in the manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard spacing between words and after punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard line should have a 3-em space between all words not separated by other punctuation than commas, and after commas; an en-quad after semicolons and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em-quad after periods, exclamation, and interrogation points concluding a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow specified space widths after different punctuation marks per this system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for adjusting spacing when justifying lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary to reduce spacing in a line, begin with commas and letters of slanting form (large shoulder); if necessary to increase spacing, begin with overlapping letters (kerns) and straight letters and points other than periods and commas, in that order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides order of priority for adjusting spaces to maintain evenness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion limits for spacing variation in well-spaced lines
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-spaced line with a 3-em space between a majority of words, there should not be more than an en-quad between the rest; maintain this proportion when increasing or reducing spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures visual uniformity across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrasting extreme spacing between adjacent lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide-spaced one, or vice versa, if avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistency across successive lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never hair-space or em-quad to avoid run-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Never hair-space, or em-quad, a line to avoid a run-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid artificially compressing lines with minuscule spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not space out last line of a paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph allowing an indentation of an em or more at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep paragraph endings visually compact; avoid trailing gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short words spacing parity
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words like 'a', 'an', etc., should have the same space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain equal spacing around short words to avoid visual oddity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin spaces after certain symbols and before metric symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, % and similar signs; before «, » "ff." and the metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "§14. Be it further ordained..."; pp. 10 ff.; 16 cm.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between currency symbols and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between symbols ($, £) and the numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $2.75; £10 3s. 2d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals at the beginning of lines and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines denoting subsections there should be an en-quad. After such numerals at the beginning of center-heads there should be an em-quad. Small-cap headings should have an en-quad between the words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings, two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines spacing norms for numbered subsections and various heading styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing format for scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced as: II Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5—3:12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the illustrated spacing and punctuation for scripture citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between product letters and superior/inferior figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical/chemical notational spacing guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation norms by measure and type size
rubrics_metrics.description: Indentation amounts vary by measure width and type size: in measures <10 picas indent all sizes 1 em; in measures 10-20 picas indent varying ems by point size (detailed table provided); similar table for hanging indentions with larger em values for larger measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed em/point rules provided for plain paragraphs and hanging indentions; follow the tables given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules for poetry and verse
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry center the longest line and let indentation be governed by that; if the longest line is disproportionate strike an average of long lines. Indent according to rhymes and length of lines; align blank verse; align consecutive rhyming lines or indent alternates appropriately; indent short lines more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and several stanza formatting variations given to illustrate rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for plain paragraphs and use of hanging indention for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter plain paragraphs are preferable. Use hanging indention to bring into relief the opening word(s), paragraph numbers, or where a center-head makes more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanging indention recommended for emphasis and longer center-heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads and slugs definitions and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary lead is 2 points thick. A slug is a thicker strip used in page make-up, standard sizes 6 and 12 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter with leads is called leaded; without leads is solid. Most books are leaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-head formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: A center-head is a headline placed at equal distances from both margins; usually set in caps or small caps. For multi-line center-heads use inverted pyramid (2-3 lines) or hanging indention (more than 3 lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided of center-head forms and long descriptive-headed works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-head formatting and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A side-head is a headline placed at the side of the page or column; may be set in separate line (flush) or run-in with the paragraph (more common). Side-heads are most frequently set in italics with only the first word and proper names capitalized; sometimes in caps and small caps or bold-face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of side-head forms: Side-head — A side-head is...; SIDE-HEAD. — A side-head is...

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-in head definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A cut-in head is a head placed in a box cut into the side of the type-page, usually set in different type and typically placed under the first two lines of the paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to emphasize or separate introductory matter; illustrated in manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box-head definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A box-head is a head for a column in a ruled table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See table-box head rules (242).
